hints: Focus on what boiling actually breaks, intermolecular forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bonds inside them.
Count the total electrons in $\text{PH}_3$ and in $\text{HCl}$, and check whether either can form hydrogen bonds with N, O or F.
Remember that F is more electronegative than O, so think about number of hydrogen bonds per molecule rather than strength of one bond to explain $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ vs $\text{HF}$.
walkthrough:
**Recall what controls boiling point**

Boiling separates molecules from each other, so it overcomes intermolecular forces. It does not break strong covalent bonds like $\text{H-F}$ or $\text{H-Cl}$.

Rule: stronger intermolecular forces = higher boiling point.

**Sort the hydrides by type of force**

$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{HF}$ can hydrogen bond because H is bonded to very electronegative O or F. $\text{PH}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$ cannot, so they only have permanent dipole-dipole forces plus instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces.

That is why $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (373 K) and $\text{HF}$ (293 K) boil much higher than $\text{PH}_3$ (185 K) and $\text{HCl}$ (188 K).

**Explain the two pairs**

For $\text{PH}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$, count electrons: $\text{PH}_3$ has $15 + 3 = 18$ and $\text{HCl}$ has $1 + 17 = 18$. Same electron number gives similar London forces, plus similar dipole-dipole forces, so very similar boiling points.

For $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ vs $\text{HF}$, F is more electronegative than O, so an individual $\text{HF}$ hydrogen bond is actually stronger. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ boils higher because each water molecule can form two hydrogen bonds on average, while each $\text{HF}$ forms only one on average.

**Pick the correct statement and reason**

Only the explanation based on equal electrons and similar intermolecular forces for $\text{PH}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$ is fully correct. The other reasons wrongly deny London forces, wrongly use covalent bond energy, or wrongly claim $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ hydrogen bonds are individually stronger.

options.A: The comparison of boiling points is true, $\text{PH}_3$ is much lower than $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, but the reason is false. $\text{PH}_3$ has no hydrogen bonding, but it must have instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces, as all molecules do. This is a common trap of forgetting London forces are universal.
options.B: The comparison is true, $\text{HF}$ boils higher than $\text{HCl}$, but the reason is false. Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. $\text{H-F}$ bond energy is irrelevant here. The real reason is hydrogen bonding in $\text{HF}$ versus only dipole-dipole plus London forces in $\text{HCl}$.
options.C: The comparison is true, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ boils higher than $\text{HF}$, but the reason is backwards. The question stem says H-bond strength increases with electronegativity, and F is more electronegative than O, so each $\text{HF}$ hydrogen bond is stronger. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ wins because it forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule, about two versus about one for $\text{HF}$.
options.D: Both parts are correct. $\text{PH}_3$ and $\text{HCl}$ each have 18 electrons, so their London forces are very similar in strength. Neither forms hydrogen bonds, so both rely on similar dipole-dipole plus London forces, giving almost identical boiling points of 185 K and 188 K.
